sections.heading: B&R vs Horticulture: Which CPWD Registration Category Should You Choose?
paragraphs: If you've started looking into CPWD contractor registration, you've probably already hit this fork in the road. CPWD doesn't just ask "do you want to register?" It asks you to pick a category first — Buildings & Roads, or Horticulture. And here's the thing nobody tells you upfront: pick the wrong one, and you don't get a warning. You get a rejected application, and you start the whole thing over.

That's not a small mistake. It can cost you weeks, sometimes months, plus a fresh enlistment fee. So before you touch the CEMS portal, let's sort out exactly what these two categories mean, who they're actually for, and how to know which one fits your business.

CPWD splits every contractor into one of two buckets. Not three, not five, but two. Everything else, including the classes, the tendering limits, and the fees; all of that sits inside whichever category you choose.

This is the big one. Most contractors applying to CPWD land here. B&R covers general civil construction like buildings, roads, bridges, and it also pulls in specialised trades like electrical work, HVAC, and mechanical fit-outs when they're tied to a construction project.

Think government office blocks, hospitals, residential quarters for staff, highways, and repair or maintenance work on existing structures. If your business pours concrete, lays roads, wires buildings, or installs air conditioning systems in government structures, you belong here.

B&R has nine classes, from Class V (the entry point) all the way up to Class I (Super), which lets you bid on projects worth up to ₹650 crore. That's a huge range, and it's built that way on purpose: a two-person firm just starting out and a national infrastructure company both fit somewhere on that ladder.

This one surprises many first-time applicants. Yes, CPWD actually runs a whole separate registration track for greenery. Landscaping, garden development, tree planting, lawn maintenance, nursery work, and the general upkeep of green spaces around government buildings; all of it falls under Horticulture.

It sounds like a small niche. It isn't. CPWD maintains gardens, lawns, and green belts around thousands of government properties, ministries, residential colonies, defence complexes, hospitals, and even Parliament-adjacent buildings. Somebody has to keep all of that alive and looking presentable, and that somebody needs to be an enlisted Horticulture contractor.

Horticulture has five classes, from Class IV up to Class I(A), with tendering limits that go up to ₹3 crore. Smaller ceiling than B&R, sure, but that also means smaller entry barriers, which is worth knowing if you're just starting out.
Here's where the two categories really diverge. Same idea — classes based on your financial strength and experience — but completely different numbers.

Notice something? Even the top Horticulture class, Class I(A) at ₹3 crore, sits below the middle of the B&R ladder. That's not CPWD undervaluing green work — it's just that horticulture contracts are naturally smaller in scale than, say, building a hospital wing. A garden maintenance job rarely runs into crores the way a road project does.

The enlistment fees follow the same pattern. B&R fees run from ₹3,000 at Class V up to ₹40,000 at Class I (Super). Horticulture fees are lighter across the board, from ₹2,000 at Class IV up to ₹7,000 at Class I(A). Both are paid through the BharatKosh portal, so the payment process itself doesn't change. Only the amount does.
Numbers on a table only tell half the story. Let's look at what these tenders actually look like once they're published.

These are the projects you'd expect: constructing a new office building, widening a road, repairing a bridge, or handling the electrical and HVAC installation for a government hospital wing. A Class III B&R contractor, for example, might bid on a ₹3 crore renovation of a CGHS dispensary building. A Class I contractor might go after a ₹40 crore highway repair package.
